#6390. About three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023 had CTE

A new study estimates that about three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023 had CTE, even after accounting for brain donation bias.

Almost every former NFL player’s brain that researchers have examined has shown signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the degenerative disease tied to repeated hits to the head.

The study estimated that families were more likely to donate a player’s brain if he had clear cognitive symptoms.

Researchers at Boston University have now worked out how much that choice skews the picture.

The team’s estimate: about three in four NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE. That includes the roughly five in six whose brains were not examined.

Three in four is lower than the figure from donated brains alone, where more than nine in ten had the disease. But the researchers said the skew in who donates can’t explain the high rate away.

Julia Gallini, a doctoral candidate in biostatistics at the Boston University School of Public Health, led the analysis with Yorghos Tripodis, a professor of biostatistics there.

Colleagues at the university’s CTE Center, Mass General Brigham and the Concussion & CTE Foundation joined them.

The figure applies to players after death only and says nothing about living former players or current ones.

Gallini said a precise number helps size the problem.

“An estimated 75% prevalence among NFL players who died over a 16-year period is concerning, and suggests we need to increase efforts to support families, diagnose CTE during life, and treat CTE-related symptoms,” she said.

CTE can only be confirmed after death, by examining the brain. So nearly everything known about it in football players comes from brains donated to a bank in Boston, and a 2017 study of 111 of them found CTE in 110.

Families don’t donate at random. A player who grew confused or forgetful in his last years is the one whose family thinks to call a brain bank.

So the donated brains carry more disease than the full population of former players would.

Epidemiologists call this selection bias. Earlier attempts to allow for it could only bracket the true figure somewhere between roughly 10% and 100%.

The team started with every former NFL player who died between January 2008 and December 2023, 2,362 men in all.

They were found through the National Death Index, the national register of death certificates. Of those, 396 had donated their brains and 1,966 had not.

The death certificates gave the researchers one fact they could compare across both groups: whether dementia was recorded as a cause of death. It was for 19.3% of donors and 11.2% of the others.

Because many people with failing memory die of something else, the team widened that category using survey estimates of milder cognitive trouble in former players.

Then they ran the comparison 1,000 times to capture the uncertainty.

The result was a ratio. A former player with clear cognitive symptoms was about five times as likely to have his brain donated as one without them.

Donors also died younger, at 67 on average against nearly 75. They had played longer too, seven years against under five.

Among the 387 donated brains with a clear verdict, 362 had CTE, or 93.5%.

After adjusting for differences in donation likelihood, the researchers estimated that 74.5% of all 2,362 players had CTE at death.

The team then tested how much that number depended on their assumptions. They restricted the sample to players who died at 55 or older, then 60 or older, and tried other definitions of who counted as symptomatic.

Across those versions, the estimate ranged from 70% to 86%.

The main figure sat toward the lower end of that range. The most conservative analysis put the figure at 63.7%.

Suppose symptomatic players had been ten times as likely to donate, rather than five. Even then, the authors calculated, more than 60% of the dead players would have had the disease.

CTE in the brain is not the same as symptoms in life.

Using the same correction, the team estimated that 27.2% of the players had a history of dementia before they died. In the donated group alone, the figure was 64.9%.

The authors said the true lifetime figure is probably higher than 27.2%. The donors it rests on died about eight years younger than the other players, with less time to develop dementia.

Many of the brains with CTE, they added, may have been at an early stage and symptom-free at death.

Matt Hasselbeck, an 18-year NFL veteran who serves as an ambassador for a research study called DIAGNOSE CTE, said the numbers read to him like a scouting report.

“I can’t take back the hits I took, but I can sign up for research and do whatever I can to help the scientists so they can find a cure in my lifetime,” he said.

The correction rests on a stand-in. Death certificates and survey estimates of memory trouble stood in for a direct look at the players whose brains were not examined. Dementia is also often left off a death certificate.

The authors also could not say whether CTE itself shortens life. That is one more reason the estimate stops at the dead and does not reach anyone still living.

Nothing here covers college or high school players, whose death records and symptom surveys don’t exist in the same form.

The authors said those estimates would be far harder to build, and that building them matters for sizing the problem.

Tripodis said the group recognizes the findings may worry living players and their families.

“Discoveries from the brain bank have already brought us significantly closer to a diagnosis during life, at which point our most important goal will be to develop effective treatments for CTE,” he said.

Until a living player can be tested for CTE, the dead are the only ones who can be counted.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

#6388. Solo meerkats can find their way back home

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Meerkats live, forage and raise their young in large groups. But they’ve still got solo skills

To test meerkats’ solo navigating skills, researchers outfitted the animals with GPS trackers, separated them from their packs, and followed their journeys back home.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.)

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6387. How one barley variety defends itself against crop pests and the virus they spread

In lab tests, fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel barley, and those that did struggled to feed. The variety also slowed the buildup of barley yellow dwarf virus.

Aphids are known to feed on the sap of barley plants. During feeding they can also transmit barley yellow dwarf virus. Plants infected with this virus become yellow and stunted and produce less grain.

In response, breeders have introduced DNA from a wild relative of barley into commercial crops. Its protective effect was believed to operate mainly after the virus had entered the plant.

This wild DNA is carried by a commercial hybrid known as SY Kestrel. A new study found that the hybrid also makes it harder for aphids to settle and feed.

The aphids avoided its smell and fed poorly on its leaves and they also produced fewer offspring.

The research was carried out by Rumiana Ray’s group at the University of Nottingham. Scientists from Keele University and Syngenta were also involved in the project. SY Kestrel itself was developed by Syngenta.

Funding for the study came from Syngenta, and two of the authors are employed by the company.

All of the experiments were conducted on young plants in growth rooms and insect cages rather than in farm fields.

“What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that resistance is not simply about stopping a virus once it enters the plant. We have found that barley can defend itself at different stages of the aphid-plant interaction,” said Professor Ray.

In severe cases a winter barley crop can lose as much as 50% of its yield to the virus. According to the UK’s Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board, losses of this size are uncommon.

Chemical control is expected to become less effective over time. The authors linked this to growing insecticide resistance in aphids and to their lengthening migration periods.

The bird cherry-oat aphid is regarded as the main carrier of the virus. It picks up the virus from an infected plant and passes it on when it moves to a new one.

SY Kestrel contains a block of DNA from Hordeum bulbosum, which is a wild grass related to barley. Within this block lies a resistance region known as Ryd4Hb.

Earlier research had linked this region to the blocking of the virus once an aphid had delivered it.

For comparison the researchers used a second hybrid named Tektoo.

This hybrid was bred from the same mother line and from a very similar father line. Unlike SY Kestrel, it carries none of the wild DNA.

Aphids from a single laboratory colony were used throughout the experiments on both hybrids. Part of this colony had been allowed to acquire the virus beforehand while the remainder was kept virus free.

In the first experiment, 20 winged aphids were released into a cage that held one plant of each hybrid.

The positions in which the insects settled were then recorded at intervals over the following 24 hours.

Six cages were used in this test and the entire experiment was later repeated in full.

More than 75% fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel than on Tektoo.

A large part of this difference could be attributed to the smell of the plants. In a separate test the air surrounding each plant was collected and offered to aphids with no plant present.

Under these conditions the insects were attracted to the odor of Tektoo but moved away from that of SY Kestrel.

The chemicals that made up each odor were then examined individually by the research team.

Heneicosane was one compound that was present in the air around Tektoo but absent from SY Kestrel. Aphids were attracted to heneicosane and those exposed to it subsequently produced a greater number of young.

In the air around SY Kestrel two compounds were detected that were not released by Tektoo. When they were tested separately both of these compounds were shown to repel the insects.

Infection with the virus was also found to alter the scent of Tektoo plants. Virus-free aphids preferred the odor of infected Tektoo plants while virus-carrying aphids preferred that of healthy plants.

This reversal has been interpreted in earlier studies as manipulation of the insect by the virus it carries. In SY Kestrel no comparable reversal could be detected by the researchers.

The odor of this hybrid repelled both groups of aphids regardless of whether the plant had been infested.

Despite the repellent odor a number of aphids did eventually settle on SY Kestrel.

Their feeding behavior was studied by attaching each insect to a fine gold wire. With this method the electrical signals from the mouthparts of each aphid could be recorded inside the leaf.

The recordings showed that aphids on both hybrids were able to reach the tubes that carry sugary sap. No meaningful difference was found between the two plants in how readily these tubes were reached.

After reaching the sap the aphids on SY Kestrel spent a longer time releasing saliva into the tubes. Sustained drinking of sap in bouts longer than 10 minutes was also markedly reduced on this hybrid.

This impaired feeding was associated with a reduction in the number of offspring produced.

On SY Kestrel the winged aphids carrying the virus produced about 40% fewer young than on Tektoo.

The survival of wingless aphids was also lower on SY Kestrel and their reproduction was reduced as well.

It is well established that plants rely on chemical defenses for protection against insects. In the leaves of SY Kestrel higher levels were found of three compounds that later proved harmful to aphids.

Each compound was tested by adding it to an artificial diet on which aphids fed for three days.

The compounds reduced the survival of aphids that were free of the virus. Aphids carrying the virus were less sensitive, and one of the compounds had no clear effect on them.

The team next examined plants that had been fed on by aphids carrying the virus. Fewer symptoms were seen on SY Kestrel than on Tektoo.

The amount of viral genetic material in the leaves of SY Kestrel was also much lower. By the tenth day the virus could no longer be detected. This measurement was based on three samples from each group.

The virus therefore faced three separate barriers in SY Kestrel.

Fewer aphids settled on the plant in the first place. The aphids that did settle fed poorly, and the virus they delivered failed to build up.

“Rather than relying on a single barrier, the crop can discourage aphids from settling, interfere with their feeding and restrict the virus they transmit,” Ray said.

The efficiency with which each leaf converted light into energy was measured as well.

This conversion represents the first step of photosynthesis and readings were taken daily from the second to the ninth day.

By the ninth day a decline in this efficiency had been recorded in Tektoo. The decline occurred in Tektoo whether or not the aphids feeding on it were carrying the virus.

A different pattern was observed in SY Kestrel when it was attacked by aphids carrying the virus.

In those plants the efficiency of light conversion remained close to the level recorded in plants without aphids. Feeding by aphids that were free of the virus did lower efficiency in SY Kestrel.

Changes in gene activity and leaf chemistry were recorded at the same time. Immune genes were involved in these changes along with the chloroplasts in which photosynthesis is carried out.

A group of fat-derived molecules that serve as stress signals in plants was affected as well.

According to the authors the continued function of the chloroplasts may help SY Kestrel to sustain its defense signals.

Several other plant viruses are already known to target the same chloroplast proteins. This has not yet been demonstrated for barley yellow dwarf virus.

SY Kestrel and Tektoo are not genetically identical outside the wild DNA. For this reason the authors acknowledged that some differences between the hybrids may originate elsewhere in their genomes.

The block of wild DNA carried by SY Kestrel is also considerably larger than the Ryd4Hb region itself. In a 2024 study, barley lines carrying a much smaller piece of this wild DNA were examined.

Complete resistance to the virus was observed in those plants. However, there was little evidence that this resistance depended on any change in aphid behavior.

Considered together, the two studies suggest that the smell and feeding defenses may depend on other genes.

Such genes may be located within the larger wild block or in other regions of the plant genome. They have not yet been identified.

The question is important for plant breeding. According to the authors, a smaller wild block may still provide strong resistance to the virus. Some of the defenses against aphids could be lost in the process.

“Understanding these complementary mechanisms offers new opportunities to develop crop varieties with broader and potentially more durable resistance,” Ray said.

Dr. James Melichar is the Hybrid Cereals Portfolio Lead Europe at Syngenta.

“This research demonstrates the value of bringing together commercial breeding expertise and fundamental plant science to understand how resistance operates in crops,” said Dr. Melichar.

“Identifying complementary mechanisms that affect aphid behaviour, feeding and virus infection provides valuable insights for developing barley varieties with broader and more effective protection.”

The diet tests also have a limitation. In these tests the levels of each compound were estimated from extracts of whole leaves.

Such estimates may not reflect the levels present in the sap that aphids actually consume.

Further research will be needed to identify the genes behind the defenses against aphids. The levels of the compounds in the sap itself will also need to be measured.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl, but they are most known for their iconic howl.

The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place?

Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network.

Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other."

However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said.

When a wolf pack howls together, they are sometimes advertising their territory to deter other packs. "Data shows that packs howl more in the center of their territory; they howl more when there are pups around and also when they have a carcass from a hunt," Tamás Faragó, an ethologist and bioacoustician at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, Hungary, told Live Science. "So group howling can have a repellent effect on neighboring packs."

However, "most chorus howling is social — that is, they howl together to build what is technically called social cohesion," Kershenbaum said, "because it makes them feel good to be safe and surrounded by their pack mates. Faragó noted that this kind of group howling gets a pack in the same mood, "and is quite common before going out on a hunt."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Howling can trigger more howling. "When an individual wolf hears a howl, it has a very strong tendency to reply back," Faragó said. However, "if a lone wolf is accidentally wandering into the territory of its neighbors, and they hear the pack there howling, they won't respond. That would make it obvious that it's an intruder there."

A wolf's howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) away in open terrain, according to the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. The combination of low- and high-frequency sounds that make up howls ensures that "even if some of the lower-frequency sounds are attenuated by vegetation, the higher-frequency components can remain intact and carry a lot of information about the individuals that made the howls," Faragó said.

Wolf pups make their first high-pitched attempts at howling between 2 to 4 weeks old.

Wolf howls differ among species and subspecies. A 2016 study of 13 species and subspecies of wolves, jackals, coyotes and dogs by Kershenbaum and his colleagues found that each has a kind of howling dialect that features different types of howls with varying regularity depending on the species or subspecies. For example, the howling repertoire of the timber wolf (Canis lycaon) is dominated by low, flat howls, while red wolves (Canis rufus) most frequently use high, looping howls.

The howling of dogs, which are descended from gray wolves (Canis lupus), can differ from wolf howling, but this depends very much on the breed. A 2023 study from Kershenbaum, Faragó and their colleagues found that more ancient dog breeds that are more closely related to wolves howl more often. In contrast, more modern dog breeds bark more often.

A question "that we all want to answer" is whether howling sounds might differ depending on their purpose, Kershenbaum said. "The problem is that most of the time when wolves howl, we don't know what they're doing at that time — they're either too far away, or it's nighttime."

Generally, "we believe that howls made in different emotional states probably sound different," Kershenbaum said. "For example, perhaps when a wolf is feeling threatened in a territorial conflict, the howl goes up and down in pitch in a different way than when the wolf is relaxed. But this is a field of active research."

A common belief is that wolves howl at the moon. "A myth, I'm afraid," Kershenbaum said. "There doesn't seem to be any correlation at all between them." He suggested that perhaps before electric lights, people were outdoors more often when there was a bright moon, "and that's when they heard the wolves."

#6385. Young emperor penguins spend their first year at sea alone, so where do they go?

Satellite tags tracked young emperor penguins from three Antarctic colonies, revealing where they roam and when proposed marine protections could help.

Juvenile emperor penguins are left to fend for themselves at sea for roughly a year after they fledge.

The young birds receive no guidance from their parents during this time and many do not survive it.

Their routes were still found to be strikingly similar in a study of three colonies around Antarctica’s Weddell Sea.

The recurring pattern can help planners estimate when juvenile penguins would spend time inside proposed marine protected areas.

The study was led by Émile Brisson-Curadeau, a postdoctoral researcher at the Centre for Functional and Evolutionary Ecology (CEFE).

Daniel Zitterbart of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution was a co-lead author. Céline Le Bohec of CEFE and the Centre Scientifique de Monaco shared that role.

“We were struck by the remarkable consistency of the penguins’ movements,” Brisson-Curadeau said.

Fishing vessel tracks were mapped as well, although the effect of fishing on the birds’ food was not measured.

Emperor penguins raise their chicks on sea ice that is attached to the coast of Antarctica.

The chicks develop waterproof feathers by late December and then leave for the open sea on their own.

Satellite tags were attached to 48 juveniles at the point when their new feathers had fully grown in.

A total of 28 birds came from Atka Bay at the eastern end of the Weddell Sea.

Around 8,000 pairs breed at that colony and its chicks were tagged over three summers between 2018 and 2023.

The remaining 20 juveniles were taken from Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula on the western side of the sea.

Each of these two colonies supports about 4,000 breeding pairs and their chicks were tagged during a single summer.

The movements of young emperor penguins from the western Weddell Sea had never been documented before this work.

Each tag was secured to the back feathers with tape and glue and weighed under 3% of body mass.

Most tags logged a position every four hours. Twelve of them also carried a pressure sensor for dive depth.

On average the juveniles travelled about 1,050 miles (1,688 km) from their colony at the farthest point of the trip.

The broad outline of this journey had already been described in earlier work carried out at Atka Bay.

No one had checked if it stayed the same across years, or across colonies on both sides of the sea.

In late summer, juveniles from Atka Bay, Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula all swam north.

By March, most had reached the waters just south of the Polar Front.

Here, cold Antarctic water meets warmer water from the north, and nutrient-rich upwelling feeds plankton and fish.

New sea ice starts forming in April. The penguins turned south to meet it and kept close to it all winter.

The ice reaches its greatest extent in August and September, and the birds moved north with its edge.

Once the ice began to melt, they headed back toward the continent.

By late December, most of the juveniles still being tracked had returned to waters near the coast, where they are thought to molt.

Multiple years of tracking were only available at Atka Bay, which made a direct comparison between years possible there.

Birds tagged in the same year were spread about as far apart as birds that were tagged in different years.

The authors suggest the juveniles may be following two stable features, namely the Polar Front and the sea ice edge.

From April onward the position of the penguins was closely linked to how far north the sea ice extended. Before April the birds were swimming in open water that lay far away from any sea ice.

A total of 52,710 dives were recorded by the pressure sensors over the course of the study.

The average dive reached a depth of about 220 feet (68 m) and lasted a little more than three minutes.

The deepest dive recorded in the study went down to roughly 1,155 feet (352 m).

Dives tended to be shallow at night and deeper during daylight hours. Deeper dives were also observed farther north and where more of the sea surface was ice covered.

The authors wrote that the birds may feed on lanternfish when they are near the Polar Front.

These small deep-water fish contain more energy than the krill and silverfish eaten by breeding adults closer to Antarctica.

Two marine protected areas are already in place in the region and two more have been put forward. The Weddell Sea proposal has been developed by Germany and the European Union since 2012.

If adopted it would become the largest marine protected area in the world and include waters near all three colonies.

Juveniles from the western colonies already spent part of their time in existing protected areas. This share was 20.6% for Snow Hill Island birds and 29.3% for Jason Peninsula birds.

Atka Bay birds spent only 2.3% of their time in such zones by comparison.

Atka Bay juveniles spent 31.6% of their tracked time in waters covered by the proposed protected areas.

Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula birds spent 21.0% and 14.7% of their time there.

Use of the proposed areas peaked in January, during the fledglings’ first weeks at sea.

Death rates among inexperienced juveniles are high in those first weeks at sea so the timing matters.

“Most marine protected areas in Antarctica are planned with penguin colonies in mind,” Zitterbart said.

“They protect the areas around the colonies, which is critical for adult penguins, but they fail to cover the sea areas where juveniles spend their vulnerable early years.”

Any new protected area in these waters needs the approval of every member of CCAMLR. This commission was set up in 1982 to conserve Antarctic marine life including krill.

Its members gathered in Hobart in October and left without agreeing on any new protected areas.

The main fishery in the region is aimed at Antarctic krill, which are small shrimp-like animals eaten by emperor penguins.

To estimate overlap the researchers relied on Global Fishing Watch, which is a public dataset of vessel activity.

It uses ship tracking signals to identify where fishing vessels are likely to be operating.

Fishing hours were totaled within about 62 miles (100 km) of each penguin location for the preceding year.

The waters used by juveniles from the two western colonies had more recorded fishing activity in the preceding year than the waters used by Atka Bay juveniles.

Much of this activity took place near the Antarctic Peninsula and in the waters around South Georgia.

Most of the overlap for these western birds occurred outside the boundaries of the planned protected areas.

Around Atka Bay the fishing effort stayed low for most months of the year.

January was the exception since the birds then used zones that had been fished heavily in 2022 and 2023.

Those zones are located within the proposed protected areas. Krill fishing there would be restricted to research and capped at one metric ton per vessel per year.

For comparison a typical fishing vessel in the region harvests about 40,000 metric tons over a year.

“Sustainable management of fishing activities, particularly their timing and intensity in key foraging areas, is essential to securing the food emperor penguins need and limiting the risk of bycatch,” Le Bohec said.

Around one third of the global breeding population of emperor penguins is found in the Weddell Sea region.

The IUCN moved the species to Endangered in April after projecting that its numbers will halve by the 2080s.

That projection rests largely on the expected loss of Antarctic sea ice.

The study measured overlap in space and time and not the direct effect of fishing on penguin foraging.

According to the authors direct studies of foraging success would give stronger evidence for the value of protection.

Tag losses also reduced the sample as the year went on and only 10 tags still reported in month 12.

Dive data were only available until September because none of the dive-recording tags transmitted beyond that month.

Sea ice extent was relatively stable between 2018 and 2024 including during an El Niño year.

Under continued warming the Polar Front is expected to contract toward Antarctica and winter sea ice could decline.

Juveniles might then travel shorter distances north but struggle to find suitable ice in winter.

A southward contraction would also raise overlap with the planned zones that are concentrated near the continent.

According to the authors it remains to be determined whether this would offset the effects of climate change.

Accelerometers could be used in future work to link penguin foraging success with fishing pressure.

Foraging and breeding success could also be compared before and after protected areas come into force.

The Weddell Sea proposal has not been adopted and most of the juveniles’ year is spent outside protected waters.

The full study was published in the journal Biological Conservation.

#6382. Permanent daylight saving time could send millions of kids to school in the dark

A new study estimates that permanent daylight saving time could add more than 2 billion trips to school before sunrise each year across the U.S.

Permanent daylight saving time sounds like more daylight. The hour doesn’t come from anywhere new, though.

It moves from the morning to the evening, and from November to March that would have millions of American schoolchildren leaving home before the sun is up.

Researchers at the University of Washington counted what that would mean, school by school, in 14 of the 19 states that have already approved the change.

The bill behind it, the Sunshine Protection Act, has passed the U.S. House but not the Senate, so the count is of a future that hasn’t happened yet.

Horacio de la Iglesia is a professor of biology at the university and the study’s senior author.

“It’s called the ‘Sunshine Protection Act’ because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act,” said Professor de la Iglesia.

Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral scholar in biology at the university, led a team that collected the actual start time of 16,093 public schools serving 8.6 million children.

Enrollment and locations came from the National Center for Education Statistics.

The team then worked out sunrise at each school on every school day. They ran it under three clocks: today’s system of switching twice a year, permanent standard time, and permanent daylight saving time.

A commute counted as dark if a child would have to leave home 20 minutes before the bell and sunrise hadn’t happened yet. The team added those mornings up across every child in every school.

Across the 14 states, permanent daylight saving time would add about 356 million dark school mornings a year compared with the current system.

Extended to every public school in the country, with a fixed 8 a.m. departure, the figure is 2.14 billion extra dark commutes a year.

In an interview with Earth.com, Professor de la Iglesia said the effect would reach nearly everyone.

“Parents should know that the number of mornings that their kids will go to school in the dark will increase dramatically under permanent DST. This will be true for virtually all children,” he said.

The hardest-hit places are not the northern ones. Georgia, which already has 75 million dark commutes a year under the current clock, would have 146 million.

Washington state would go from about 20 million to 55 million. Mississippi and Alabama, where schools start before 8 a.m. on average, would each go from about 2 million to more than 20 million.

What matters is where a school is inside its time zone. Sunrise comes later on the western edge of a zone, so Georgia, at the far west of Eastern Time, gets darker mornings than Maine at the far east of it.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him most when the state numbers came in, Professor de la Iglesia named that pattern.

“That some of the hardest-hit States are not necessarily in a high northern latitude, like Georgia,” he said, and he put it down to Georgia’s position in its time zone.

Rodríguez Ferrante, who answered alongside him, said the average student in Georgia would leave for school before sunrise on about 86 school days a year under permanent daylight saving time.

In Washington state, much farther north, she said the figure would be about 52.

For a single child in Washington, the change is 28 to 39 more dark mornings a year, depending on the grade level.

The team then turned to a decade of fatal crash records, 2015 through 2024, from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s FARS database.

They kept only school-year weekdays between 7 and 8:30 a.m., which left 10,305 fatal crashes, and 1,754 of them involved a pedestrian.

“Among fatal crashes during the morning school commute, the percentage involving a pedestrian aged 5 to 18 roughly doubled before sunrise,” Rodríguez Ferrante told Earth.com.

She said the analysis does not show that most such crashes happen in the dark, only that the crashes before sunrise more often involved a school-age pedestrian.

The figure for children rests on 141 crashes, so its range is wide.

The crash records show a pattern, not a cause. The authors wrote that the analysis is observational, that it counts only fatal crashes, and that the far larger number of non-fatal collisions is not in the record.

School districts have spent years pushing high school start times later because teenagers’ body clocks run late.

Permanent daylight saving time would move every start time an hour earlier relative to the sun without changing a single bell schedule, which the authors wrote would reverse those gains.

Morning light also does a job of its own. It helps set the body clock that regulates sleep, mood and appetite, and a child who leaves in the dark misses that cue.

De la Iglesia said he has heard the argument that schools could simply start later under permanent daylight saving time.

His answer was that everything else would then shift later too, work included, until everyone was back on solar time, which is what standard time already is.

“The U.S. tried year-round DST in 1974, and abandoned it within the year, partly because of dark winter mornings and concern for children traveling to school,” Rodríguez Ferrante said.

The count assumes every child leaves 20 minutes before class, and the national estimate assumes an 8 a.m. departure everywhere.

Both choices are on the late side, so the authors wrote that the true number is likely higher.

Children who arrive early for a school breakfast program, who are more often from lower-income households, would lose more mornings than the count shows.

The study estimated how often children would leave before sunrise. It did not measure how those darker commutes would affect their sleep or grades.

Rodríguez Ferrante said the bill passed the House in July and has stalled in the Senate, which adjourned for the midterm elections without acting on it.

The full study was published in the journal Current Biology.

#6381. A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Unlike in the Dr. Seuss tale, a swollen heart can be an alarming sign of stress or disease

The Grinch’s change of heart turned him from grumpy to radiating joy. Is such a transformation possible in real life?

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

“They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand says, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”

Stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson says.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.)

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as big as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”

#6380. Brain scans reveal a surprising pattern in teens who spend more time on screens

A study of 44 Finnish teens linked more screen time to smaller gray matter volume in a memory region and larger volumes in some other areas.

Earlier studies on teenagers and screens have generally associated longer device use with reduced gray matter in the brain.

Gray matter is the brain tissue in which the bodies of nerve cells are concentrated.

That familiar pattern was also observed in a memory region by a team studying Finnish teens aged 16 to 19.

In regions involved in attention and planning, however, more gray matter was found among the heavier screen users.

These results are difficult to interpret because gray matter volume typically decreases as the teenage brain matures.

The research was led by Hannamari Skog, a doctoral researcher at the University of Eastern Finland‘s Institute of Biomedicine.

Her team scanned the brains of 44 teens on a single occasion each.

Habits and brain features that occur together can be identified with this design. Proof that screens altered anyone’s brain cannot be obtained from it.

The participants were recruited from the Physical Activity and Nutrition in Children study in Kuopio in Finland. They had taken part in that project for eight years.

A total of 277 teens attended the project’s eight-year checkup and 60 of them were invited to the brain study.

Those invitations were extended so that the full range of performance on a sprint test would be represented.

Forty-six teens agreed to participate. Two of them were later excluded when structural brain abnormalities were detected on their scans.

The final sample consisted of 25 girls and 19 boys who each underwent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain.

Specialized software estimated gray matter volume in 102 regions of the outer brain and in 10 deeper structures.

Screen use was assessed by questionnaire. Daily hours on phones, tablets, computers, TV and videos were reported by the teens themselves.

The reported average was 9.2 hours per day and about 5.2 of those hours involved phones and tablets.

Individual totals ranged between 2.5 and 19 hours and each figure rested on the teen’s own estimate.

The content viewed on the screens was not assessed by the questionnaire. Only the number of hours was recorded.

Fitness was measured with a standing long jump and a shuttle run that covered 164 feet (50 meters) in total.

Teens who reported more screen time had less gray matter in the medial temporal lobe. This inner part of the temporal lobe is involved in memory and learning.

The same link was found for time on phones and tablets alone. It appeared on both the left and right sides of the brain.

Age, sex, head size and body fat were taken into account. The links still held.

In all, the team ran 72 statistical tests. With that many tests, a few links can appear by pure chance.

So a correction was applied to the results. The memory region links survived it.

Skog’s team had predicted this result. The temporal cortex matures late, they wrote, and is particularly sensitive to environmental influences.

For the authors, the finding raises concerns, because the region is implicated in memory disorders.

“Excessive screen time and smart device usage may be harmful to the areas of the brain that are involved in memory and learning,” Skog said.

The researchers had also expected teens with more screen time to have smaller frontal regions.

Teens with more screen time had larger volumes in two frontal regions. One helps the brain plan movements.

The other is part of the prefrontal cortex. It supports working memory, planning and decision-making.

Total screen time was also tied to a larger area in the occipital lobe. That lobe processes vision.

Time on phones and tablets was linked to larger volumes in two more frontal regions.

“The larger volume in these areas may be particularly related to applications and games that require attention, motor planning and visual information processing,” Skog said.

Some researchers split screen time into active and passive kinds. Active use includes problem-solving or interactive play. Passive use means simply watching.

A 2019 study cited by the team made this kind of split. Gaming was linked to a larger prefrontal cortex in that work.

Social media use was linked to a smaller temporal lobe. The Finnish questionnaire did not distinguish between time spent gaming and time spent on social media.

An earlier analysis from the same Finnish project had a related result. Some working memory scores were higher among teens with more screen time.

A larger region should not be assumed to be a better one. The prefrontal cortex is also one of the last regions to fully mature.

“During normal brain development in adolescence, there is a reduction in grey matter volume and an increase in brain efficiency,” Skog said.

“The positive link between screen time and the volume of grey matter in these areas may thus also reflect a delay in brain development.”

That idea was not tested in this study. Only one scan exists for each teen.

How each teen’s brain changed over time was therefore not recorded.

Larger temporal and frontal volumes had been expected in active and fit teens, but this pattern did not appear.

The teens reported 92 minutes of physical activity a day on average. More activity was tied to a larger region in the right occipital lobe.

But that link was no longer statistically significant after the correction.

Fitter teens had a larger left parietal lobe. This region helps process sensation and attention.

Better fitness was also linked to smaller volumes in the right hippocampus and one other region.

Neither of those two links remained after the correction, and the authors wrote that both may be chance findings.

Part of the weak result may be explained by exercise intensity, which was not captured by the questionnaire.

The authors wrote that teenagers’ everyday activity may be too light to influence brain volume.

Each teen was scanned just once. So the study can’t show whether screen habits came before the brain differences or after.

The group of 44 was small and not typical of all teens. Most had a parent with a polytechnic or university degree.

No data on sleep or diet were collected. Either factor could explain part of the pattern.

Skog’s team collected the data in 2018 and 2019. Screen habits may have differed then from the habits seen today, the authors wrote.

The survey recorded screen time by device or broad category, but it did not break down how much time teens spent on specific activities.

Those hours could have been spent on games, videos, schoolwork or social media.

Screen-time apps could capture that detail, the authors wrote, and wearable sensors could measure how hard teens exercise.

“The results provide new information on how everyday lifestyle factors, such as screen time, physical activity and physical fitness, are linked to brain structure in adolescence,” Skog said.

“However, in light of the results, the connections between lifestyle factors and brain structures in adolescence are complex, and more research is needed to understand their long-term significance.”

The authors called for larger studies that follow teenagers over years, to clarify whether different kinds of screen use cause differences in the brain.

The full study was published in the journal NeuroImage: Reports.

A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers in Japan have developed a new technology that could enable electric vehicles (EVs) to charge "simply by parking".

Wireless charging is still relatively nascent in the EV market, but scientists hope that integrating more wireless charging devices into roads and parking spaces will move the EV industry away from bulky plug-in infrastructure. It uses the same wireless power transfer technology found in modern smartphones and consumer electronics: a transmitter coil inside in a ground pad generates an oscillating magnetic field, which induces an electric current in a receiver coil underneath the vehicle. This current recharges the EV's battery cells.

However, small misalignments between the two coils can affect how quickly and efficiently the battery recharges. This new system uses short-range radio signals to determine the position of the vehicle's magnetic charging coil relative to the charging device in the ground, including its distance and angle. This helps the EV and its driver get into the optimal position for efficient charging.

The technology could be particularly useful for driverless "robotaxis" and other autonomous vehicles that need to be able to recharge quickly and efficiently without human assistance, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study published Aug. 26 in the IEEE Open Journal of Vehicular Technology.

"We hope this research will lead to a future where EVs charge simply by parking, much like smartphones placed on wireless chargers," Ryotaro Hada, first author of the study and a master's student at the University of Osaka's Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, said in a statement.

Existing methods for aligning an EV's charging coil with a wireless charging pad use magnetic sensors or cameras. Magnetic systems work best when the coil is close to the pad, while cameras can struggle in rain, poor lighting or when dirt obscures the pad, the researchers explained.

This new system uses four ultra-wideband radio devices mounted around the vehicle's charging coil to communicate with four antennas around the charging pad.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By measuring how long radio waves take to travel between the ultra-wideband devices and the antennas, as well as detecting tiny differences in how the signals arrive at each of the vehicle's sensors, the system can pinpoint the position and angle of the EV's charging coil relative to the ground pad.

The same technology is used in some digital car keys. They use short radio pulses to detect when the driver is close by, allowing the driver to unlock their vehicle without requiring a physical key.

In laboratory experiments using a scaled-down vehicle model, the system worked out where the vehicle's charging coil was to within 0.09 inches (2.32 millimeters) of its actual position and which direction it was facing to within 0.25 degrees. Correcting for distortions in the radio signals reduced the positioning error by around fivefold, the team said.

The researchers noted that the system still needs to be tested outdoors, on full-size EVs and under real charging conditions.

#6377. Migrating birds may be bringing unusual ticks to Hungary

Volunteers in Hungary found 29 Hyalomma ticks over five years, raising the question of whether the ticks are starting to breed there.

Hyalomma ticks can carry the virus that causes Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a serious and sometimes life-threatening illness. They usually live in warm, dry places, but lately they keep turning up in Hungary.

For five years, scientists in Hungary have been asking people to send in any of these ticks they find.

What they’ve learned so far raises a simple question: are the ticks just passing through, or are they starting to settle in?

At the HUN-REN Centre for Ecological Research in Budapest, Éva Szabó, Gábor Földvári and their colleagues in the Eco-epidemiology Research Group run the project.

Hyalomma ticks usually live in warm, dry parts of Africa, the Middle East, Asia and southern Europe.

Young Hyalomma ticks often feed on birds, including birds that migrate long distances. Adult Hyalomma ticks feed mostly on large animals such as cattle and horses.

The way these ticks feed helps explain how far they can travel. A young Hyalomma tick usually stays on the same animal while it grows.

For Hyalomma marginatum, that’s about three weeks. Ixodes ricinus, the most widespread tick in Hungary, lets go after less than a week each time.

The authors linked the ticks’ spread north to climate change.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control keeps a map of where Hyalomma marginatum has turned up in Europe.

Scientists watch these ticks closely because of a virus some of them carry.

The World Health Organization names Hyalomma ticks as the main carrier of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. The study’s authors wrote that it’s the most important tick-borne virus affecting people.

How many people get sick from it each year isn’t clear, because many infections cause no symptoms. The authors cited an estimate of 10,000 to 15,000 cases worldwide.

The World Health Organization estimates that 10% to 40% of reported cases in outbreaks are fatal.

A vaccine has seen limited use in Eastern Europe, and no vaccine is widely available. Treatment relies on supportive care.

Hyalomma ticks hunt their hosts instead of waiting on plants. Dragging a cloth through vegetation, the traditional way to collect ticks, doesn’t work well for them.

So the team relies on citizen scientists instead.

The researchers opened a website called TickWatcher in April 2021.

Four years later, they added a free phone app called PragmaTick. People send in a photo of an odd-looking tick, and an expert checks it.

By late November 2025, the website had about 107,000 visits. The app had been downloaded 2,500 times. Volunteers had made 1,014 submissions, and 29 turned out to be Hyalomma ticks.

The app won’t accept a report without a date, a place and a photo.

In the app’s first six months, people sent about as many reports through it as they had sent by email in the four and a half years before.

“Successfully involving the public in research can even help unravel problems like finding a needle in a haystack,” the authors wrote.

Thirteen of the 29 ticks were on horses. Five were on buffalo, two on dogs, one on a donkey and one on a cow, and reports came in between mid-June and the end of October.

Horse owners tend to check their animals closely and ride through grass and woods, which may help explain why horses topped the list, the researchers wrote.

News about the program may also have reached some groups of people better than others.

Even so, the authors concluded that owners of livestock and other large animals are likely more affected than other groups.

Three ticks came from people. Four more ticks were crawling with no host, including the one on the kitchen floor.

Most of the 29 were males, 21 in all. One possible reason, according to the authors, is that males may stay on a host longer while they look for mates.

At a buffalo farm near the village of Ágasegyháza, people found four Hyalomma ticks in 2022 and one more in 2023.

Two other finds came from within about 9 miles (15 kilometers) of the farm. One was on a cow in 2021, and the other turned up in a garden near the city of Kecskemét in 2023.

All 18 ticks that people mailed in tested negative for the virus. The other 11 were thrown away or destroyed by the people who found them.

Earlier studies in Hungary found antibodies against the virus in 10 of 2,700 people tested between 2008 and 2017, and in 11 of 1,905 cattle and sheep tested in 2017.

Antibodies show past exposure, not a current infection, and these tests may also react to related viruses.

The biggest open question is whether these ticks are only passing through or starting to survive and breed in Hungary.

Answering that will take time. The team plans to keep collecting reports, with close attention to livestock owners and to places where several ticks have already been found.

For now, the people in the best position to help are the ones already checking their horses and cattle.

Every tick they send in shows scientists a little more about where these ticks are turning up.

The full study was published in the journal Current Research in Parasitology and Vector-Borne Diseases.

#6375. Extreme heat is killing more people, and scientists have estimated how much warming is to blame

A Lancet Countdown report found that annual heat-related deaths rose 36% worldwide, with human-caused warming accounting for more than two-thirds of the recent toll.

The Paris Agreement took effect in 2016. From 2016 through 2023, an estimated 540,800 people died from heat worldwide each year, on average.

That was about 36% higher than the annual average from 2006 through 2015.

The share of heat-related deaths attributed to human-caused warming rose from 55% to 68%.

A project based at University College London, the Lancet Countdown, produced the figures in its tenth annual report, which tracks 54 measures of how climate change affects health.

It was written by 146 researchers and produced with the World Health Organization. Every death count in it is an estimate from models, not a tally of death certificates.

In an interview with Earth.com, Jennifer Israelsson, a senior research fellow at the Lancet Countdown, said the finding that surprised her most was not a number from the heat data.

It was “the sharp decline in political engagement with the climate-health agenda, despite multiple years with record-breaking temperatures, deadly heatwaves and devastating flooding events across the globe, and the intensification of hurricanes,” Israelsson noted.

Between 2006 and 2015, heat was linked to an estimated 398,400 deaths a year. Between 2016 and 2023, it was linked to 540,800 a year, with a range of roughly 369,000 to 681,000.

Near the end of that stretch came the worst year. Heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths in 2023, and the authors attributed 71.5% of them to human-caused warming.

The researchers attributed an estimated 2.96 million heat-related deaths to human-caused warming from 2016 through 2023.

Annual heat-related deaths attributed to human-caused warming rose by an average of 7,400 per year from 2006 through 2015. From 2016 through 2023, they rose by an average of 15,600 per year.

The researchers used daily temperatures and death records reported at daily, weekly or monthly intervals across 129 countries. They then used models to estimate the global toll.

The second question was how many of those deaths would have occurred in a world with the same weather minus the warming humans have added.

The authors call the gap between the two the attributable toll. The attribution step is new to this year’s report, and the ranges around each figure are wide.

Heat also keeps people from working. The authors estimate 573 billion potential work hours were lost to heat in 2025, 35% above the average for 2006 to 2015.

The lost income came to $1.07 trillion, about 0.9% of global economic output.

The losses were equivalent to 5% of GDP in countries with a low Human Development Index and 0.5% in countries with a very high index.

The same decade brought real gains. Investment in clean energy reached a record $2.1 trillion in 2025, 82% more than went into fossil fuels.

The share of electricity from modern renewables rose from 5.5% in 2016 to 13.5% in 2023. Fossil fuels still supplied 80.7% of the world’s energy in 2023.

Where air pollution from fossil fuels fell, the authors counted the benefit. In 75 of 140 countries assessed, cleaner air prevented an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.

Air conditioning tells a mixed story. Its use grew from 32% of households in 2016 to 42% in 2024, and the authors estimate it prevented more than 360,000 heat deaths in each of 2022 and 2023.

In countries with a low Human Development Index, only 3% of households had air conditioning in 2024.

Israelsson told Earth.com the single change that would save the most lives from heat is a heat-health action plan.

That means a warning system that reaches hospitals and the public in time, plus measures for cooler buildings and safe working conditions.

She pointed to the Netherlands, which she said has seen heat deaths fall since it adopted a heatwave plan.

Extreme drought covered 51.8% of the world’s land for at least a month in 2025, the second-highest extent on record after 2023.

Since 2016, the area in drought each year has grown about eight times as fast as it did in the previous decade.

Very heavy rainfall affected an average of 17.2% of the world’s land each year from 2016 through 2025, up from 14.8% in the previous decade.

Such downpours can increase the risk of floods, landslides and waterborne disease.

The number of people affected per storm or flood rose more slowly in countries with health early warning systems.

The annual increase was 8.6% smaller than in countries without those systems.

Whether the acceleration continues is the open question, and the authors wrote as much. The heat figures run only through 2023, and the drought and rainfall trends through 2025.

The authors’ answer is to have climate change formally declared a global health emergency.

Israelsson said the WHO’s existing emergency mechanism was built for short, acute outbreaks like Ebola and “is not designed for long-term emergencies.”

A new instrument with the same kind of roles and responsibilities, aimed at long-term resilience, is needed, she said.

“A decade after the Paris Agreement, our findings are unambiguous: the health harms of climate change are growing faster than the world’s response to them, and in many cases even accelerating,” said Marina Romanello, the Lancet Countdown’s executive director.

The report was published ahead of the COP31 climate talks.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet.

#6374. The Book Lover’s Gift Guide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Science News staff loved books about dinosaurs, parenting and numbers in 2026

Science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor

Big thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” says senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a new appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with new parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Company | $29.99

Adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham says.

Senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen says. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, new mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she says. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century New England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00

Conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover says. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole new light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”

And for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”

#6373. Webb looked at a giant black hole from the dawn of the universe and saw something unexpected beside it

Webb spotted a faint light beside a giant black hole just 900 million years after the Big Bang, and astronomers think it may come from a second black hole.

Giant black holes from the young universe still puzzle astronomers. Now a team has found what looks like two of them, close together and both feeding.

The pair, nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, dates to just 900 million years after the Big Bang.

If confirmed, it would be the closest-spaced quasar pair known from cosmic dawn.

A quasar is the brilliant glow produced as gas falls toward a supermassive black hole. That glow can outshine all the stars in its galaxy combined.

Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, led the study.

Her team thinks pairs like this one may mark places where young galaxies were crowding together, feeding new stars and fast-growing black holes at the same time.

The researchers lean toward two real quasars. They haven’t ruled out, though, that the fainter one is a copy of the brighter one, made when light bends around a galaxy in between.

“There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two,” Onorato said.

“We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.”

The universe’s first billion years, a period astronomers call cosmic dawn, were busy.

Clumps of dark matter collapsed, galaxies made their first stars, and the first supermassive black holes took shape at the centers of the biggest galaxies.

Galaxies back then often ran into each other, and some merged completely.

When galaxies collide, gas can funnel toward their central black holes. The gas heats up as it spirals inward, producing the light we see from a quasar.

Since galaxies collided so often, astronomers expect plenty of quasar pairs closer together than the width of a typical galaxy.

So why have so few turned up? Part of the problem is timing, since a black hole shines as a quasar for only a short part of its life.

Distance is the other problem. Quasars from cosmic dawn are so far away that they look faint and are hard to detect from the ground. And when two of them are very close together, it’s hard to tell one from the other.

Those hurdles make Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua a rare find. If confirmed, it would be the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn.

The pair’s Hawaiian name was created through the A Hua He Inoa program at the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi. The University of Hawaiʻi’s Hawaiian Language College, Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani, also took part.

In English, the name means “Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.”

Astronomers found the pair in the Aether survey, a James Webb Space Telescope program that’s taking a census of objects in the early universe.

Emanuele Paolo Farina, an associate scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini, leads the survey.

Farina’s team used Webb to split the light of 200 quasars into its colors, point by point. That’s 43% of all the quasars known from this stage of cosmic history.

Onorato’s team checked every one by eye. Next to J1602+4228A, a quasar first reported in 2004, they spotted a second, fainter source. No other quasar in the survey had a companion like it.

The faint one, J1602+4228B, is so dim and so close to its partner that seeing it from the ground should have been nearly impossible.

Earlier Gemini observations from a 2017 program had pointed only at the brighter quasar.

The team went back with Gemini North, a telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawaiʻi, and recorded each quasar’s light separately.

“The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights,” Onorato said.

The brighter quasar’s black hole weighs about 1.5 billion times as much as the Sun. Its partner’s comes in at about 400 million, roughly a quarter as heavy.

As seen from Earth, the two are about 18,100 light-years apart, or about one-fifth the width of the Milky Way.

The two quasars’ light was stretched by almost exactly the same amount on its way here, which means they’re at nearly the same distance from us.

Both black holes are pulling in matter near or slightly above the Eddington limit. At that point, light from the falling gas pushes outward about as hard as gravity pulls inward.

Feeding that fast is typical for quasars this early, the researchers wrote.

The fainter quasar also looks redder, a sign that more dust is blocking its light.

Could the second quasar be a copy of the first? A massive galaxy between Earth and a quasar can bend the quasar’s light and make two or more copies of it. Astronomers call this gravitational lensing.

To test the idea, the team looked at light from gas spread across hundreds of light-years around each black hole.

Stars inside a lensing galaxy can distort light from a small area near a black hole, but not from gas spread that widely.

The light from the gas showed different patterns in the two spectra. The brighter source showed a stronger signature of gas flowing outward.

The researchers wrote that this difference favors two separate quasars.

Older Hubble images do show a galaxy near the line of sight to the fainter quasar, which could hold the extra dust or act as a lens. Its spread-out look suggests it’s fairly close to us, making strong lensing unlikely.

Even so, the team wrote, spectra alone can’t definitively rule out lensing.

Based on how quasars cluster over larger distances, a pair this close should be extremely rare.

Yet one turned up among the 199 quasars the team searched around. That’s roughly 100 to 1,000 times more clustering than the predictions suggest.

Predictions at such small distances are very uncertain, though, and one pair can’t show whether close pairs are really this common.

“Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment,” Onorato said.

“It’s a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.”

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
