#6338. The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

Be prepared for unexpected power failures and off-the-grid camping trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

We evaluated eight power stations of varying sizes, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed its listed max output to see how well it could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using its AC adapter, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with more than five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

Bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts (with 3,900-watt startup power) and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

We hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-watt starting power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

The Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

A new and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

The Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

Performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

This power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

What is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

The S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

One of the standout features of Bluetti’s Apex 200 is a maximum solar input of up to 3,000 watts. You rarely find that much input power for a station of this size. There are two sets of DC inputs for this: low-voltage XT60 input (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 input (up to 2,000 watts). If you have the panels and enough perfect direct sunlight to achieve this full potential, you could fully charge this station in less than two hours using the sun’s rays.

Beyond that, the Apex 200 is a fairly robust power station, with 3,200 watts of continuous power. (It says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery.) I ran my refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and when I tested it for battery efficiency, I estimated it at about 90 percent, which is very good for a power station. There’s also a 120-volt 30-amp output if you wanted to run a few circuits in your home by hooking up to a manual transfer switch. Just keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

The 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity isn't huge—at least not for home backup—but you can expand it by adding up to six additional batteries. That could add up to over 33 kilowatt-hours if you use the largest batteries Bluetti offers, the B500K. That’s massive.

Even with all this power, the Apex 200 is still a fairly portable station. Weighing 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. So, when you’re not using it for home backup, it’s perfect for taking on a long outdoor trip or for powering an RV when a site hookup is not available.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review

This is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

The unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The S5000 is the second power station in Anker's S-series, which features inverter efficiency technology that helps to reduce wasted energy when the inverter is idling or running lower-powered devices. We were impressed with how this technology performed in the S2000, and this model matched that performance.

We ran this through several tests, and the battery efficiency proved to be around 97 percent (the industry average is around 89 percent). For example, we left the AC inverter idling for 18 hours, and the battery remained at 100 percent capacity. Meanwhile, another station we idled at the same time lost 19 percent of its available power. That was impressive.

The next most impressive attribute about the S5000 is its size. It’s at least half the size of other power stations that feature 5,000 watt-hours of capacity and includes just as many outputs, including a 240-volt, 30-amp outlet. It also has both high- and low-powered DC inputs that enable up to 3,000 watts of solar power input if you have the panels to generate that. You can also recharge at up to 4,500 watts using a direct DC connection to Anker's 5500 Smart Tri-Fuel generator.

With only 4,500 watts of total output, we wouldn’t call this a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that), but the S5000 can deliver a decent amount to power an RV, run lights and appliances during an emergency, or even a couple of critical circuits.

During our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

This 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and new outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

We loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

As part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

The mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

We should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

In testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

Recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

The Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the important information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

All of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easiest to use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via WiFi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge for a full eight months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you plan to plug into it.

Some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds when you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048-watt-hour capacity and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

Keep in mind that the usable watt-hours are not the same as the watt-hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

These days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

While all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Midsize models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Large portable models can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

Portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large-capacity power station that will back up critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn inputs off and on and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

Often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that they stay charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, this can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or run the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most new portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

That depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

Some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you plan on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

#6337. How do tumors talk to nerves? This scientist is finding out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Sebnem Ece Eksi wants to see how nerves change as cancer progresses. She hopes those changes could offer clues for detecting tumors earlier.

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”

Eksi now plans to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

“This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi says. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”

#6336. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 21: Mercury far west of the Sun

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 20: The Moon passes Saturn and Neptune

If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

Located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — currently larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

If you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

A stunning new image from the Gemini North telescope captures two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity, helping to trigger the birth of new stars.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What it is: NGC 7253 (also called Arp 278), a pair of interacting spiral galaxies

Where it is: 200 million light-years away, in the constellation Pegasus

Picture a spiral galaxy, and you'll probably imagine a swirl of stars. But some galaxies appear to be the complete opposite. One is NGC 7253, which looks more like a bizarre balloon animal than a cosmic coil. In reality, it's two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity. As shown in this recent image from the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii, the galaxies' once-ordered shapes are being disturbed and disrupted as their mutual gravitational pull stretches and distorts their spiral arms into a tangled arrangement of stars, gas and dust. It sounds and looks chaotic and destructive, but encounters between galaxies don't mean stars are physically colliding; the distances between individual stars are too great. Instead, something extraordinarily productive can happen.

Spiral galaxies contain huge clouds of cold gas and dust, particularly within their arms. When galaxies interact, gravitational forces can disturb and compress those clouds. If enough material is squeezed together and becomes dense enough to collapse under its own gravity, it can produce bursts of new star formation.

Evidence of just that can be seen in this image. Scattered through the galaxies are concentrations of bright pink light. These are H II regions — enormous clouds of hydrogen gas energized by intense ultraviolet radiation from hot, young stars.

The gravitational encounter is rearranging two structures containing billions of stars while simultaneously helping to create new ones. These interactions radically alter the shapes of the galaxies involved and, in time, can ultimately cause them to merge into a single galaxy. For now, NGC 7253 is listed as Arp 278 in the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies, a catalog of galaxies that are neither perfectly symmetrical spirals nor smooth, spherical ellipticals.

The new image has another story much closer to Earth. It's just been given the Hawaiian name Nā 'Uhane Māhoe Huki Pū i ke Ola, meaning "The Twin Spirits Pulling Together Creating Life." Hawaii high school students participating in the 2026 Project Hōkūlani internship program chose the name. One reason was its position within Ka Lupe o Kawelo, the Hawaiian constellation corresponding to Pegasus.

The "twin spirits" represent both the two galaxies and the twin telescopes of the Gemini Observatory — one in Hawaii and the other in Chile.

#6332. How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Cornell computational social scientist Yian Yin turns the tools of science on science itself. He’s studying how AI-assisted submissions are changing what gets through peer review.

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.

He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

#6331. Nov. 21, 1993: The death of Bruno Rossi

Born in Venice, Italy, in 1905, Bruno Rossi attended the University of Bologna, graduating with a doctorate in physics in 1927. When race-based laws inspired by his country’s growing closeness with Nazi Germany meant the Jewish Rossi had to leave Italy, he made his way to the U.S. In 1940, Rossi became an associate professor of physics at Cornell University, and from 1943-1946, he worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos Laboratory. After the war, Rossi joined the faculty of MIT, where he remained until his retirement in the early ’70s.

Throughout his long career across countries and institutions, Rossi laid the groundwork for the study of several key fields in astronomy and astrophysics. His research into cosmic rays became the basis of high-energy particle physics, while his pioneering search for cosmic X-rays jump-started X-ray astronomy. Rossi also conducted trailblazing research into the interplanetary medium, and contributed to the development of public policy for space exploration. Rossi passed away at age 88 on Nov. 21, 1993. Today, among other honors and memorials that Rossi accrued, the Bruno B. Rossi Prize for astrophysics is awarded yearly.

#6330. Scientists Studied Thousands of Ancient Skeletons and Found a Strange Truth About Human Progress

Over 7,000 years, height rose and fell across Europe and Asia. Food quality, not tech, made the difference.

The dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

“When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”

To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

In China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

Trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan said. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

In Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

Women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

The authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

“Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” said Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, new, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”

Europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

Going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” said Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”

#6329. What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, asks how changes in the way people care for the land may have left it more vulnerable to wildfire.

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”

#6328. The Sky Today on Sunday, November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

Zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

Stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Astrophysicists have dared to ask a cosmological question never asked before: Do black holes "wear pants"? New research shows how fast-spinning black holes may split apart.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black holes are known to collide and combine in monstrously violent merger events, but new research suggests these celestial stalwarts can also fragment into smaller bodies, like a cosmic pair of pants splitting down the middle.

In a paper published Oct. 22 in the journal Physical Review D, researchers used several mathematical modeling methods to propose a "pair-of-pants" topology for black holes. The hypothesis suggests that under extremely specific conditions, these dark behemoths could fragment into numerous less-massive black holes.

"Understanding precisely what is forbidden, what is merely unlikely, and what becomes possible once the assumptions are relaxed is the central goal of this work," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Black hole fragmentation could play into other cosmic mysteries. For example, it could help to explain black holes with masses that are too small to be formed through conventional astrophysical processes. These hypothesized black hole "morsels" would be so small that astronomers could see them evaporating before their eyes on observational timescales.

In the new paper, the researchers explored whether black holes' event horizons — the boundaries beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape — could split under various cosmological conditions. These situations included classical four-dimensional general relativity (Einstein's description of our large-scale universe as we currently understand it) as well as cosmologically esoteric frameworks such as higher-dimensional space-time and modified gravity scenarios.

But modeling black hole dynamics, especially the split of an event horizon, is messy work. So the researchers simplified it by comparing discrete slices of space-time, effectively condensing the fragmentation process into static snapshots from before and after the split.

In our classical cosmos, it seems mostly impossible for black holes to split, the researchers found, but they did identify a loophole that might allow it to happen.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The "pair-of-pants" topology for the fragmentation of a black hole.

The first impediment is entropy, the possible arrangements of an isolated system's energy, which cannot spontaneously decrease but only stay the same or increase. This has been theorized by Stephen Hawking and recently demonstrated through detections of ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, suggesting that a black hole's surface area cannot decrease.

For these reasons, splitting a static Schwarzschild black hole — the simplest type of black hole in our four-dimensional general relativity — would be strictly forbidden because it would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

The second impediment is kinematics, the motion of orbital dynamics, which precludes the possibility of a permanent split because the black hole fragments would recombine into a single body incredibly quickly.

But there is a loophole: A rapidly rotating black hole could literally spin itself apart.

"This is why, in four-dimensional general relativity, an isolated black hole in empty space could only split if it spins very close to the maximum rate the theory allows, what we call a near-extremal black hole," study co-author Manuel Del Piano, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southern Denmark, told Live Science via email. "Loosely speaking, the equator of the horizon is then dragged around at nearly the speed of light."

Through this theoretical process, the two resultant black hole fragments could be gravitationally slingshotted away from each other before they could recombine. So under conventional space-time conditions, it seems "black holes do not wear pants."

Then, the researchers mathematically modeled black hole fragmentation in versions of space-time with more than four dimensions.

In models of higher-dimension space-times, a black hole's rotational velocity is no longer limited because gravity weakens with increasing dimensionality. Therefore, any such ultrafast spinning black holes could theoretically fragment, the researchers explained in the paper.

A diagram from the new study illustrating the theoretical pants-splitting method.

In the "black string" model, a normally spherical black hole would become cylindrical or string-like, stretching across any extra dimensions. It could then pinch off to fragment into multiple smaller bodies, akin to "beads on a string."

Additionally, the researchers calculated that black hole fragmentation may be entropically favored in space-time models with modified gravity, which alter the gravitational interactions in extremely warped environments near the black hole.

"The fragments are tiny, though: in one of our benchmarks, a black hole of ten solar masses would favour fragments … a few times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza squeezed into a region smaller than a proton, and the heavier the parent, the smaller the fragments," Del Piano explained.

Fragmentation also may be more likely if there is a "bumpy horizon" around black holes, akin to a dense blanket or shroud of exotic matter that acts as a singular-but-gigantic quantum entity. The superfluid qualities of this matter could create strange vortices that eventually cause a black hole to fragment into multiple smaller bodies.

Scientists might see a black hole decrease in size, an actual fragmentation, or simply an indirect gravitational signature, depending on the dimensions and whether it intersects the viewer's "brane," or slice of dimensionality.

The researchers expect that smaller objects — like the hypothesized, miniature primordial back holes that may have formed shortly after the Big Bang — are more likely to split, compared with much more massive astrophysical black holes such as those at the centers of galaxies.

"Overall, we expect small black holes, such as primordial ones from the early universe, to be the most prone to splitting," Del Piano told Live Science.

Gamma-ray telescopes or gravitational wave observatories may one day offer evidence of a signal associated with the supposed split of a small black hole, but the specifics, including whether this actually occurs, are uncertain.

"One important caveat: our analysis shows when splitting is allowed by entropy and conservation laws, not that it actually happens," Del Piano noted. "As we put it in the paper, a shattered glass has more entropy than an intact one, yet glasses don't shatter on their own. Settling the question requires full dynamical simulations, which is the natural next step."

Cacciapaglia, G., Del Piano, M., Sannino, F., & Vellucci, V. (2026). When black holes admit pair-of-pants topologies. Physical Review. D/Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/cx69-t466

#6324. This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve quickly

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

MIT computer scientist Dor Minzer uses math to prove when there’s no computational shortcut. He now guides graduate students through the kinds of problems that drew him to the field.

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says. “You have to really be curious.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”

Minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

“I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”

#6323. The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

He has good reason to believe this marvel of ancient Rome may surpass all modern concrete methods.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

For decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

Masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he says he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

Scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

But it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

Then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first big clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic says. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

Masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

The research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic says. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

Originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

What the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

While lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When the concrete is exposed to water, the calcium spontaneously expands, creating a protective layer of nanoparticles that fill in the cracks before they can spread. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

The team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

Roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less new material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

Our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, says Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

In fact, Masic co-founded a company in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also plans to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. #6321. Nov. 22, 1942: The birth of Guion Bluford

Born Nov. 22, 1942, in Philadelphia, Guion “Guy” Bluford went on to major in aerospace engineering at Penn State. In addition to training as a fighter pilot in the Air Force, Bluford also earned master’s and doctoral degrees from the Air Force Institute of Technology. In 1978, he was selected to be a space shuttle astronaut in Astronaut Group 8 — one of just 35 people chosen from 10,000 applicants.

Bluford launched as a mission specialist on Challenger for STS-8 on Aug. 30, 1983, becoming the first African American in space. Three additional space shuttle missions would follow, bringing Bluford’s total time in space up to 688 hours – including NASA’s first night launch and night landing of the space shuttle and the largest crew in space (eight people on one spaceflight). In 1993, he retired from the military and NASA; today he continues to work in the private sector of the aerospace industry.

Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades.

Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C.

The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said.

The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said.

During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground.

"This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, said at a news conference, according to local news outlets. She added that the last similar find was made in Hungary in the late 1960s.

The hoard's silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms — a very early type of large silver coin that was introduced in the late sixth century B.C.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The newfound Celtic tetradrachm copies are a type known as "Velem," which are named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum. Similar coins have been found at that site, which is located about 10 miles (15 kilometers) to the west.

Each coin has a stylized head on one side that probably depicts the Greek god Apollo, and portrays a helmeted rider and horse on the other side.

Artifacts from more than 7,000 years of occupation have been found at the site, including a glass bead (bottom, center) thought to be about 2,500 years old.

The excavations have revealed evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation at the site, officials wrote in the statement. The artifacts include a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel used for woodworking and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C.

A Roman-era villa was built at the same site in later centuries, without disturbing the hoard of buried silver, Kreiter said at the news conference.

The site in Hungary's western Szombathely region was excavated between 2023 and 2025 ahead of the construction of an electricity substation.

The villa has long since been demolished, but the excavations enabled the archaeological team to reconstruct its floor plan, including its underfloor heating system, she said. They also found a Roman-era brick with a dog's paw print.

The artifacts from the site will become part of a museum exhibition.

According to Museum Wales, the Celts were loosely related Iron Age peoples descended from Proto-Indo-European speakers. Emerging in Central Europe, Celtic groups occupied much of Central and Western Europe from about the 10th to the first century B.C. The Celtic Gauls were finally defeated by the Romans, led by Julius Caesar at Alesia, now in eastern France, in 52 B.C. The Britons were also Celtic, though most people of Celtic descent would not have recognized that name.

Several modern ethnic groups, including the native Irish and the Bretons of coastal France, trace their descent to the Celts. Regions with strong Celtic origins are sometimes called the "Celtic fringe" of Western Europe.

Writing in the Journal of Roman Studies, the British coin expert Christopher Howgego, an honorary curator and professor emeritus of Greek and Roman numismatics at the University of Oxford, stated that Celtic tribes in the Carpathian Basin, now in Hungary and Romania, started minting their own silver coins after Celtic mercenaries had seen them when serving with Hellenistic armies in Greece and Macedonia.

Howgego has written that the Greek-inspired Celtic coins included adaptations of classical Greek portraits, as well as distinctive Celtic designs. These copycat tetradrachms held very high value for their makers, so they were rarely used for everyday purchases. Instead, they were often hoarded as wealth or buried as ritual offerings.

#6318. Astronomer Isabel Angelo hunts for odd signals in telescope data

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A comet or a newborn star might explain an odd signal in telescope data. Astrophysicist Isabel Angelo is looking for signals that defy those familiar explanations.

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”

November's full Beaver Moon rises on Tuesday, Nov. 24, giving us a preview of the spectacular Christmas Eve supermoon coming next month.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk on Tuesday (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. Here's what's coming up:

November's Beaver Supermoon is just the beginning: It's the smallest of the three upcoming supermoons. December's full Cold Moon will be the closest, biggest and brightest full moon of 2026, bringing the moon closer to Earth than at any time since Jan. 2, 2018, according to late astrophysicist Fred Espenak.

#6315. NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a new GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

North Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

“We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.
